newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu adviser sees limited Palestinian "state". [CORRECTED 00:27 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu adviser sees limited Palestinian "state". [CORRECTED 00:27 GMT]

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's chief of communications said in an interview published on Friday that Israel might accept a Palestinian entity called a "state" under certain conditions.
David Bar-Illan told the Jerusalem Post that Netanyahu was more concerned about the powers a Palestinian entity might have than by what it might be named.

"The point is that you can call it anything you want. You can call it autonomy plus or you can call it a state minus," Bar-Illan said in an interview with the Jerusalem Post's diplomatic correspondent David Makovsky.
"While Netanyahu is making (demilitarisation) a condition for the existence of an entity -- whether you call it a state or not is not really the important thing," he said.
The right-wing Netanyahu, elected in May, has repeatedly gone on record as opposing an independent Palestinian state.

He has expressed a preference for the autonomous areas of the West Bank and Gaza Strip to have a status vis-a-vis Israel akin to the ties between the United States and its Caribbean commonwealth of Puerto Rico.

"The condition is that it cannot have unlimited sovereignty; that it cannot have an army of a quarter of a million people, produce its own nonconventional (or) conventional weapons, make alliances with radical regimes like Iraq and Iran, control the airspace over Israel, etc," Bar-Illan said.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said last month he would declare a Palestinian state in two years' time.

A five-year interim period during which Israel and the Palestinians were to seek to reach a final settlement to their decades-old dispute began when Arafat signed a peace agreement with the late Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Rabin in Washington in September 1993.

In the interview, Bar-Illan said the government's policy of strengthening Jewish settlement in lands captured from the Arabs in the 1967 Middle East war did not mean the territorial expansion of the outposts.
(Corrects to read "...war did not...", inserting dropped word "not".)
"There will be no moving of any perimeter fences," he said, adding there was sufficient room within settlements' existing boundaries to handle any population growth.
Some 130,000 Jewish settlers live amidst two million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
U.S. President Bill Clinton on Monday embraced the tough language of his predecessor George Bush this week when commenting on the settlement issue.
Asked at the White House if he would call settlements an obstacle to peace, he told reporters: "Absolutely".
